PRESENTATION OF THE TREATY. —This treatise The Perfection of Man's Justice is dedicated by Saint Augustine to the bishops Eutropius and Paul, little-known characters, who had sent him a writing, brought from Sicily, that contained the definitions or arguments attributed to Celestius.

DIVISION OF THE TREATY.—It has two well-defined parts, following the same order as that of Celestio's writing. The first part includes sixteen arguments proposed by the disciple of Pelagius; The second part explains the texts of Holy Scripture that he adduces to prove his ideas about the possibility and even ease of man to be without sin and to be just and perfect. Man, with the own forces of his will and free will, can easily avoid any sin. Saint Augustine refutes Celestio's arguments one by one and correctly explains the biblical texts, respecting, however, the very title of the writing.

Diarecritic.—Saint Augustine uses the same dialectical method as his adversary: to each of the sixteen brief and subtle arguments (n.1-16) he responds concisely and sharply, demonstrating that perfection and fullness of justice, without any kind of sin, is impossible for man with the forces of nature, now vitiated; nor can anyone achieve it in the present life without the help of grace. From number 17-44 he analyzes what Celestio's writing calls authorities (testimonia), taken from the liscritura, where man is commanded to be holy, immaculate and perfect, and, at the same time, he is reminded that God's commandments are not heavy or difficult, and even (n.23) he tries to highlight, as a contradiction of Catholics, that man alone cannot fulfill them.

LITERARY GENRE.—Saint Augustine does not say anything about this work in his Revisions, perhaps because he considered it as a letter, the series of which he planned to review apart from the books. In fact, it seems that way because of the heading, the recipients, the greeting, etc., which makes it similar to the epistolary genre.

About Julian, a heretic of the fifth century, we have very little historical data. Very imprecise, and often contradictory, news in Saint Augustine, Mario Mercator, Gennadius and Paulinus of Nola. We do not know the place of his birth. He is called Eclana because, it is believed, he was bishop of this town, in Apulia, located southeast of Benevento, near the current Mirabella Eclano. The date of his birth is set at the end of the 15th century, around 386.

His parents, Memorio, bishop of an uncertain diocese, and Juliana, were people distinguished by their nobility, their qualities and their position in society. They give their son a liberal education. An intimate friendship unites them with Paulino de Nola and Bishop Agustín Joven, with promising hopes, under the direction of his father, he studies the Latin classics; He learns Greek and begins to learn other knowledge typical of that time. His taste for dialectic is notable, Agustín has heard good things about this young man, and he asks Memorio to send it to him, given that 'xondum curis maioribus detinetur'. He traveled to Rome, and it is likely that he met the coryphaeans of Pelagianism: Pelagius, Celestius, Turbantius and Florus. He returns to his land and takes as wife the one from the Emilios family. Paulinus, future bishop of Nola, dedicates a flowery epithalamium to him?

Summary.—In this third book Augustine refutes, with arguments of reason, book 1 of Julian. It clearly proves that man is the work of God, and marriage is a good in itself, a divine institution; but the lust that covets against the spirit is evil. Marital chastity makes good use of this evil, but continence is a better good by not making use of concupiscence, which is not a nature different from that created by God, as the Manichaeans say, but is a sequel to the disobedience of Adam that is transmitted to us, and only the obedience of Christ heals it. The debt contracted at birth is forgiven, by grace, at rebirth. It also proves from Julian's own words that concupiscence is an evil, since he recognizes in his writings that effective remedies must be used to heal it and its movements must be stopped, and it is a glory to combat it with the practice of perfect continence.
